  Forty years after Godfrey and Isgur published their relativized quark model
  [Phys. Rev. D **32**, 189 (1985)], it is still the default $q\bar q$ baseline
  --- and its numbers still cannot be regenerated from the paper alone. I set

  a finite-difference solver as a first foothold, then the long way back to the
  paper's own harmonic-oscillator method and its three-stage order of
  diagonalization and mixing. Four corrections along the way --- about
  normalization and phase, about a converged approximation that was
  nevertheless the wrong calculation, about what convergence does and does not
  certify, and about verification infrastructure that reported the wrong run
  --- taught me more physics than the successful steps did. Much of the work
  was carried out with coding agents, and the false starts are part of the
  story. What the excursion left behind is a Julia package whose intermediate
  quantities can be inspected, a comparison package that keeps the provenance
  and the still-open residuals, and a course and set of notebooks for anyone

# Why I went back to 1985

The relativized quark model of Godfrey and Isgur [@godfrey1985] --- hereafter
GI --- describes light and heavy mesons, "from the pion to the upsilon," within
a single soft-QCD Hamiltonian. One fixed set of parameters produces the masses,
and afterwards the couplings, of essentially the whole meson landscape. Four
decades later it is still the baseline against which new states are judged.

What drew me in was the gap between that status and what one can actually do
with the paper. The relativistic smearing, the momentum-dependent operator
factors, and the isoscalar annihilation machinery are specified
semiquantitatively, spread across the main text and Appendix A, and the spectra
themselves appear as figures rather than tables. To use the model you must
first rebuild it, and everyone who has rebuilt it has done so privately. I
wanted to know whether the published numbers really do follow from the
published ingredients, with no fitting of my own --- and I wanted the answer to
be inspectable afterwards, by me and by anyone else.

So this is a trip report. It follows the order in which things happened: what
the paper asks you to compute (@sec-model), the route I took through it
and why it was the wrong way round (@sec-route), the four mistakes that
taught me the most (@sec-corrections), what it was like to do this with
coding agents (@sec-agents), what the reproduction currently rests on and
where it is still incomplete (@sec-evidence), and what the excursion left
behind for other people (@sec-leftbehind). Throughout, the 1985 paper is
the authority; my code is only a claim about it.

I make no claim to be the first person to program this model. The point of
doing it in the open is narrower and, I think, more useful: this particular
calculation now exists with its assumptions, its conventions, and its evidence
attached to it.

# What the paper asks you to compute {#sec-model}

## The Hamiltonian

GI start from a rest-frame equation with a relativistic kinetic term,
$$
H\,|\Psi\rangle = (H_0 + V)\,|\Psi\rangle = E\,|\Psi\rangle ,
$$ {#eq-schrodinger}
$$
H_0 = \sqrt{p^2 + m_1^2} + \sqrt{p^2 + m_2^2},
$$ {#eq-kinetic}
with $V=V(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{r})$ momentum dependent and
$\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{p}_1=-\mathbf{p}_2$. In the nonrelativistic limit $V$
reduces to the familiar sum of confinement, hyperfine, and spin--orbit terms.
The spin-independent piece combines a linear Lorentz-scalar term with a
Coulomb-type one-gluon exchange,
$$
H^{\text{conf}}_{ij}
  = -\Big[\tfrac34 c + \tfrac34 b r - \frac{\alpha_s(r)}{r}\Big]\,
    \mathbf{F}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{F}_j ,
$$ {#eq-conf}
with $\langle \mathbf{F}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{F}_j\rangle = -4/3$ in a meson; the
color hyperfine interaction supplies the contact and tensor pieces,
$$
H^{\text{hyp}}_{ij} = -\frac{\alpha_s(r)}{m_i m_j}
  \Big[\tfrac{8\pi}{3}\,\mathbf{S}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}_j\,\delta^3(\mathbf{r})
  + \frac{1}{r^3}\,S_{ij}\Big]\mathbf{F}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{F}_j ,
$$ {#eq-hyp}
and the spin--orbit interaction splits into a color-magnetic and a
Thomas-precession part. A separate gluon-annihilation term $H_A$ contributes
only in self-conjugate isoscalar channels.

As GI themselves stress, @eq-hyp and its spin--orbit companions are more
singular than $r^{-2}$ and are illegal operators in @eq-schrodinger as written.
The resolution is Appendix A, and Appendix A is where the reproduction work
actually lives.

## Relativization: smearing and momentum factors

Two things happen there. First, the relative coordinate is *smeared* over
distances of order the inverse quark masses,
$$
\rho_{ij}(\mathbf{r}'-\mathbf{r})
  = \frac{\sigma_{ij}^3}{\pi^{3/2}}\,
    e^{-\sigma_{ij}^2(\mathbf{r}'-\mathbf{r})^2},
$$ {#eq-smear}
with a mass-dependent width $\sigma_{ij}(\sigma_0,s)$, which tames the
short-distance singularities and makes the operators legal. Second, the
coefficients acquire a dependence on the quark momenta: mass factors $m^{-1}$
are promoted to operator factors built from $E_i=(p^2+m_i^2)^{1/2}$, so that
the light-quark hyperfine term saturates to a finite $m\to0$ limit controlled
by $\langle p^{-1}\rangle$ instead of diverging.

Concretely, the central Coulomb and confinement terms become their smeared
forms $\widetilde G(r)$ and $\widetilde S(r)$, and the Coulomb operator is
dressed with a Hermitian momentum sandwich,
$$
G' = A(p)\,\widetilde G\,A(p),
\qquad A(p) = \Big(1 + \tfrac{p^2}{E_1 E_2}\Big)^{1/2},
$$ {#eq-sandwich}
with the same construction, at the side exponents $\tfrac12+\epsilon_i$ of
Table II, applied to the contact, tensor, and spin--orbit kernels. Those
kernels are themselves built from derivatives of the *smeared* central
functions. Getting the ordering of these operations right, and keeping it right
in two different numerical representations, turned out to be most of the
project.

The strong coupling is a frozen sum of Gaussians,
$$
\alpha_s(Q^2) = 0.25\,e^{-Q^2} + 0.15\,e^{-Q^2/10} + 0.20\,e^{-Q^2/1000},
$$ {#eq-alphaq}
with $Q$ in GeV and $\alpha_s^{\text{crit}}=0.60$, which becomes a
coordinate-space error-function profile convenient for convolving with
@eq-smear. In self-conjugate isoscalars, $q\bar q$ annihilates through gluons
($n=2$ for $C=+$, $n=3$ for $C=-$), and the channel-coupling element
$$
\begin{aligned}
A(^{2S+1}L_J)_{ji} = {}& 4\pi(2L{+}1)\,A(^{2S+1}L_J) \\
  &\times \Big[\frac{\alpha_s(M_j^2)\alpha_s(M_i^2)}{\pi^2}\Big]^{n/2}
  \frac{S_L(\Psi_j)S_L(\Psi_i)}{m_i m_j}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ann16}
depends on the wavefunction near the origin through $S_L(\Psi_i)$. That
dependence is what later made the isoscalars the sharpest test of whether I had
the wavefunctions right, not merely the energies.

## The inputs I allowed myself

The parameters are GI Table II, taken verbatim (Table~\ref{tab:params}). These
constants, the $\alpha_s$ form above, and the paper's reference masses are the
only inputs; nothing in the model is fitted here.

```{=latex}
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{GI Table II parameters, used verbatim. The tensor exponent is the
paper's $\epsilon_f$ (code \texttt{epsilon\_t}).}
\label{tab:params}
\begin{tabular}{llr}
\toprule
Quantity & Symbol & Value \\
\midrule
Light quark mass & $\tfrac12(m_u+m_d)$ & $220$ MeV \\
Strange mass & $m_s$ & $419$ MeV \\
Charm mass & $m_c$ & $1628$ MeV \\
Bottom mass & $m_b$ & $4977$ MeV \\
String tension & $b$ & $0.18$ GeV$^2$ \\
Constant & $c$ & $-253$ MeV \\
Frozen coupling & $\alpha_s^{\text{crit}}$ & $0.60$ \\
QCD scale & $\Lambda$ & $200$ MeV \\
Smearing width & $\sigma_0$ & $1.80$ GeV \\
Smearing exponent & $s$ & $1.55$ \\
Contact factor & $\epsilon_c$ & $-0.168$ \\
Tensor factor & $\epsilon_f$ & $+0.025$ \\
Vector spin--orbit & $\epsilon_{\text{so}(V)}$ & $-0.035$ \\
Scalar spin--orbit & $\epsilon_{\text{so}(S)}$ & $+0.055$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
```

GI quote an expected accuracy of $25$ MeV for light-quark mesons and $10$ MeV
for heavy-quark systems, dominated by neglected coupled-channel shifts and by
the schematic relativization. That is the standard the reproduction has to be
measured against --- and it is worth saying early that a solver tolerance and a
physical accuracy are different things, a distinction I had to keep
re-learning.

# The route I took, and why it was backwards {#sec-route}

In 1985 the harmonic-oscillator (HO) basis was not a stylistic choice. It was
the practical route through an operator that depends on both position and
momentum: oscillator functions have tractable representations in both spaces,
and Appendix A inserts intermediate states to assemble products of the
corresponding matrix elements. The paper's procedure has three stages. The
relativized Hamiltonian is diagonalized in a large HO basis within fixed
$|jm;ls\rangle$ sectors, the basis being enlarged until convergence. The
smaller mass matrices generated by the off-diagonal tensor
($^3L_J\!\leftrightarrow\!{}^3L'_J$) and antisymmetric spin--orbit
($^3L_J\!\leftrightarrow\!{}^1L_J$, unequal masses only) couplings are then
diagonalized in the basis of those eigenvectors. Finally, self-conjugate
isoscalars acquire the annihilation matrix.

I did not start there. A finite-difference (FD) radial calculation was the
easier foothold: grid values, explicit operator matrices, and contribution
plots gave me something I could look at directly, term by term, when nothing
yet worked. That was the right first move for a first implementation, and the
wrong final answer. Once the FD spectrum stood up, its independence became the
lever for going back to native HO matrix elements, and then to the paper's own
order of diagonalization and mixing. The sequence was FD to HO, with repeated
comparison at every step --- a lesson about how *this* project went, not a
general ranking of the two methods.

The intermediate stage was the most instructive, because it looked finished
when it was not. Representing a wave in an HO expansion does not by itself
reproduce the paper's algorithm. Native operator assembly, full fixed-sector
diagonalization, and the later mixing stages all still had to be recovered
individually. The native HO path now evaluates position- and
momentum-dependent factors in their own representations, following Appendix A,
optimizes the oscillator scale, and enlarges the basis until every requested
energy passes a stated convergence test --- currently $0.1$ MeV over two
consecutive refinements, supplemented by wave-overlap diagnostics and
wave-sensitive audits. FD survives as an independent comparator, which is a
better fate than being the headline.

# Four corrections that taught me physics {#sec-corrections}

The useful part of the trip was not the code that worked. It was the code that
worked *and was wrong*, and what it took to notice.

**Normalization and relative phase.** A diagonal Rayleigh quotient is unchanged
when its input vector is rescaled; a bare off-diagonal overlap is not. So
comparing sampled FD waves with reconstructed HO waves demanded a common
physical normalization, and without it perfectly matching diagonal results
happily coexisted with badly wrong mixing matrix elements. The fix is recorded
in commit `a987862`. The HO phase-convention correction in `9ff437b` is the
same lesson from the other side: an individual eigenvector has an arbitrary
phase, but every operator and every mixed-state composition must transform
consistently with whatever phase you chose. Both are statements about physics
that I met as implementation failures.

**A converged approximation can still be the wrong calculation.** A
nonperturbative solve that was unavailable in one path had been quietly falling
back to a first-order shift. Commit `eef789b` made that case fail loudly
instead. The later fixed-sector work (`b9d3474`) put the full diagonal spin
interactions into the Hamiltonian *before* solving it, rather than adding them
afterwards. Recovering the masses was not enough: the spin-distorted
wavefunctions have to reach the decay and annihilation observables too, which
is exactly where a first-order shortcut stops being invisible. The completion
in `78a3d76` also removed extra spin-strength bridge factors once the literal
Appendix-A coefficients were correct.

**Convergence certifies less than it appears to.** Commit `8655d68` removed the
mesh from the HO Appendix-A assembly, and `39ee9c8` made adaptive basis
refinement a production requirement rather than a diagnostic. But energy
convergence had to be complemented by tests of origin-sensitive functionals and
of the final mixed-state observables --- an energy can be stable to $0.1$ MeV
while $S_L(\Psi)$ in @eq-ann16 is still moving. The independent FD
certification in `bdd65d8` gave a second numerical route with its own spacing
and domain checks, but agreement between two routes only became evidence about
the physics once I could say precisely which representations and which
approximations each of them was making.

**Verification infrastructure can hide the mistake.** Commit `959fdb0`
corrected a scorecard that was faithfully reporting the *previous* verification
run, and `2fd3fd7` restored FD/HO audits that had drifted outside the gate.
This is not a clerical detail. A correct-looking report that does not describe
the code you are inspecting is worse than no report, and keeping the reference
comparison and its generation path explicit is part of the physics, not
housekeeping around it.

# Doing this with agents {#sec-agents}

Much of the work was carried out with coding agents, and the git history
records the whole shape of it: extraction from the paper, implementation,
autonomous iterations, physics audits, repairs, and eventually teaching
material. The paper, the numerical checks, and my own reading supplied the
criteria for accepting any of it.

The honest summary is that the failure modes above are the story. Plausible
code, passing local tests, and a reassuring residual could all coexist with a
missing physical operation. What made the difference was the corrective loop:
a discrepancy raised a question about normalization, or operator staging, or
provenance; the question sent me back to the paper or to an independent
calculation; the answer changed both the code and my explanation of it. That
loop is also why the mistakes are worth writing down --- each one is a small
lesson in quantum mechanics that happens to be reachable through a diff.

These are episodes from one repository, not a controlled measurement of agent
productivity or reliability. The commit identifiers here are navigation
anchors: the changes and their audits are the evidence, not the commit titles.

# What the reproduction rests on, and where it stops {#sec-evidence}

GIPaper keeps a manifest of paper units with links to code, tests, reference
sources, and residual reports --- the detailed record of what has actually been
computed and compared. Reference data keep their origin, whether a printed
table or a digitized figure. Parameter provenance is tracked with the same
care, because taking the paper's inputs, repeating a fit the paper performed,
and calibrating a diagnostic control against reference targets are three
different operations, and only the first two are predictions. The reports label
which is which so that a control cannot quietly become evidence.

One compact example of the current state: the photon audit gives
$\mu/\mu_N=+0.688$ for $\rho\to\pi\gamma$ against the printed $+0.69$, and
$-1.200$ for $K^{*0}\to K^0\gamma$ against $-1.20$. Those are values from the
checked-in audit of September 7, 2026, not a fresh calculation made for this
manuscript. The $\rho$ row is also the row GI used to fit a relativization
exponent, so its agreement tests the reconstructed pipeline rather than
supplying an independent prediction --- exactly the kind of distinction the
provenance labels exist to preserve. Other transitions probe different flavor
weights, wavefunctions, and cancellations, and are the more interesting test.

The aim is full-depth reproduction, and the repository audit is candid that it
is not there yet: complete accounting of the Table VI photon-decay rows and the
characterization of their residuals are still open, and some mixing- and
cancellation-sensitive quantities retain visible discrepancies. So this report
does not claim exact agreement for every printed number, nor whole-paper
coverage. The native three-stage spectrum implementation and the independent FD
comparator are done and documented separately from that remaining work; the
boundary should move as the audits close, and the audit files, not this report,
are where it is authoritative.

# What the excursion left behind {#sec-leftbehind}

## A calculation you can take apart

The thing I most wanted at the start was the thing that did not exist: a
version of this calculation whose intermediate quantities you can look at. In
the model a rest-frame mass is an eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian, whose kinetic
part is @eq-kinetic and whose remainder is the confinement and spin-dependent
structure of @sec-model. When configurations mix, a physical state is
$$
|\Psi\rangle=\sum_a c_a|\psi_a\rangle,
$$
with signed coefficients and explicit flavor content, and a transition is a
coherent sum,
$$
\langle\Psi_f|O|\Psi_i\rangle
 =\sum_{a,b}c_{f,a}^{*}c_{i,b}
   \langle\psi_{f,a}|O|\psi_{i,b}\rangle.
$$
Writing it out is the quickest way to see why a mixing *probability* cannot
predict a decay: the relative phases can enhance or cancel. A width needs the
decay operator, the normalization, and the kinematics as well; the mass
spectrum alone does not determine it.

The package exposes those stages in that order. A spectrum contains
identifiable states; a state resolves into physical components; components lead
to solver-native waves; waves lead to radial matrix elements; the comparison
layer relates the result to a printed number. What stays visible throughout is
which quantity is an input, which is computed, and which is a reference value
--- the three things I most often confused with each other while getting here.

This also makes conversational use of the model reasonable: a language model
can turn a physics question into a package calculation, explain the objects
that come back, and point at the methods involved, while the numbers come from
executing the code and carry their parameters, labels, solver settings, and
convergence information with them. That is an intended use of the existing
interface, not a claim that a validated conversational product exists.

## A course, and notebooks

Somewhere along the way the reproduction turned into teaching material,
because the questions I had to answer for the code were the questions a
student has anyway. The theory course is nine sheets: radial quantum mechanics,
angular momentum and meson quantum numbers, variational and semirelativistic
methods, confinement and the running coupling, relativization and smearing,
spin fine structure, mixing, decay observables, and the complete spectrum
algorithm. Every problem has a worked solution and a short concept check. A
computational-discovery sheet starts the bridge to numerical work; the full
hands-on course is still ahead.

Each piece has its own job. The paper gives the original model and its
reasoning. The course slows the derivations down and makes you do them. The
notebooks make the assumptions adjustable and the consequences immediate. This
report is the map, and deliberately does not repeat the course.

Pluto suits the last of those: executable cells, reactive dependencies,
mathematical prose, controls, and results that redraw when you change a mass or
a solver setting. Live documentation and linked docstrings make a notebook an
entry point into the package rather than a demonstration beside it, and the
documentation graph links the public operations explicitly, with a static link
audit checking that the path from any explanation to the next numerical
question actually exists. The adaptive HO notebook turns the convergence
question of @sec-route into the lesson: it follows the oscillator scale
and the basis refinements, shows the energies settling, and asks the reader why
a curve that looks flat still needs a criterion --- and why energy convergence
does not certify every wave-sensitive observable.

## Seeing the model move

One consequence of an executable model surprised me by how much it explains.
The heavy-quark notebook varies a constituent heavy-quark mass continuously
while the shared interaction parameters stay fixed, which connects the model's
$D$ and $B$ sectors, or its $D_s$ and $B_s$ sectors, or --- varying both masses
--- charmonium and bottomonium. Subtracting the constituent rest masses
separates the change in binding and excitation structure from the plain rise in
total mass, and hyperfine splittings, level ordering, and the response of the
light degrees of freedom become things you watch rather than tabulate.

Two honest caveats belong with that picture. The heavy masses are external
parameters of a constituent model with a shared phenomenological interaction;
the interpolation is a family of model calculations, not a physical decay of a
bottom meson into a charmed one. And the same access to wavefunctions invites
structure pictures --- radial densities, nodes, characteristic radii, angular
distributions --- which are only interpretable if they say what they display:
for a normalized reduced radial wave $|u(r)|^2\,dr$ is a radial probability,
while the three-dimensional density carries the angular factor too, and mixed
states need their coherent composition and the right spin or flavor sums. The
ingredients for a curated meson-structure animation are all there; the
animation itself is not yet.

# Where I would go next {#sec-outlook}

The obvious continuations are physics rather than software. Screened
interactions [@li2009] and explicit coupled-channel treatments
[@barnes2008; @ortega2010] are the two directions in which the GI baseline has
mostly been extended, and each changes the model and needs its own validation.
Closer to hand, the paper's quark-emission operator could be applied directly
to the calculated physical wavefunctions instead of the single-oscillator-scale
approximation used for its numerical strong-decay tables --- which would expose
the role of radial nodes, state-dependent scales, and mixing in those
amplitudes. That is the test I most want to run, because it uses the
wavefunctions rather than only the eigenvalues, and the wavefunctions are what
this whole excursion was really about.

Julia makes one more direction tempting. For an isolated normalized eigenstate,
$$
\frac{\partial E_n}{\partial\lambda}
 =\left\langle\psi_n\left|
 \frac{\partial H}{\partial\lambda}\right|\psi_n\right\rangle
$$
is an explicit starting point for sensitivity studies and fitting. The
repository already contains the numerical-type preparation and FD and
fixed-scale HO derivative probes. End-to-end automatic differentiation is
future work, and not trivially so: adaptive basis selection, level crossings,
and derivatives of mixed eigenvectors all need care. Whatever comes out of it
will need the same checks the original computation did.

If there is a moral to the trip, it is the one from @sec-corrections: the
model became clear to me at exactly the points where my code was confidently
wrong. That is the experience I would like the course and the notebooks to
make available to someone else --- ask a question, get a number, take the
number apart, and find out what you had assumed.
